{#jy48} # Discussion

{#e6b0} Our study indicated that silencing PinX1 enhances radiosensitivity and antitumor-immunity of RT by enhancing IR-induced telomere dysfunction, therefore improving the antitumor efficiency of radioimmunotherapy.

{#hqjl} PinX1 was initially identified as a telomerase-binding protein with a highly potent inhibitor of telomerase activity [@w:w27]. However, many studies have suggested that PinX1 positively regulates telomere maintenance and promotes genome stability in tumor cells [@w:w28]. The role of PinX1 in tumorigenesis and progression varies widely among cancer types [@w:w29]. For NSCLC, previous studies have shown that PinX1 inhibits tumor cell proliferation [@w:w30]. Our previous studies have shown that the high expression of PinX1 induced radioresistance through promoting telomere maintenance and chromosome stabilization, and targeting PinX1 significantly enhances radiosensitivity via increasing IR-induced telomere dysfunction in ESCC [@w:w31]. In the in vitro experimental part of our study (including colony formation assay and CCK-8 assay), knockdown of PinX1 also increased cell proliferation of tumor cells to a certain extent, however, when combined with RT, cell proliferation appeared significantly downregulated relative to RT alone. {#wvwx} # Background

{#poow} Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounts for roughly 85% of all lung cancer cases and substantially contributes to cancer deaths worldwide . Both immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) immunotherapy and radiotherapy are first-line treatments for NSCLC. For locally advanced NSCLC, chemoradiation combined with ICB has become the standard treatment. [@w:w1] However, the curative efficacy of radio-immunotherapy is still suboptimal, and radioresistance remains a significant barrier to improving the antitumor-immunity of IR, limiting the survival benefit of NSCLC from radiotherapy–immunotherapy combinations [@w:w2]. Therefore, there is an urgent need to investigate prospective combination modalities to enhance the antitumor immunity of IR.

{#dgt1} Radiotherapy can elicit significant immunostimulatory effects, including triggering immunogenic cell death (ICD) and improving the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) [@w:w3]. However, there needs to be more strategies that could effectively boost the antitumor-immunity of radiotherapy in clinical settings due to inadequately elucidated mechanisms. The prevailing view suggests that radiation directly induces DNA damage and micronucleus formation in tumor cells, leading to DNA single- and double-strand breaks (DSBs) [@w:w4].
